newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-MIDDLESBROUGH AND CHESTERFIELD RUE WHAT MIGHT HAVE BEEN.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-MIDDLESBROUGH AND CHESTERFIELD RUE WHAT MIGHT HAVE BEEN.

text.p: Middlesbrough and Chesterfield were left to rue squandered leads and questionable refereeing decisions on Monday after one of the greatest English Football Association (F.A.) Cup semifinals of recent history.
Boro, for the second time in a week, let a cup tie slip from their grasp by conceding an equaliser in the dying minutes of extra time.

Chesterfield must be wondering how, after leading 2-0 with half an hour to play against a side with 10 men, they failed to book an unprecedented place in the final of the world's oldest cup competition.

And while Middlesbrough manager Bryan Robson argued that the first-half dismissal of Slovakian defender Vladimir Kinder was the turning point of Sunday's outstanding 3-3 draw at Old Trafford, second division Chesterfield could legitimately complain that they had a perfectly good goal disallowed.
On 67 minutes, with the score at 2-1 to the underdogs, striker Jon Howard rifled a shot off the underside of the Boro crossbar. The ball crossed the line before bouncing back into play.
Seconds later referee David Elleray blew for a Middlesbrough free kick although no-one appeared to have been fouled before the shot and Howard was quite clearly onside.
Elleray later acknowledged that the ball had crossed the line. Whether the free kick was given for an incident before or after Howard's shot remained a mystery.
"You make a decision which is honest from the position you're in," said Elleray, one of the game's most experienced officials. "You then have to clear your mind and get on with the game."

Whatever the truth, Chesterfield manager John Duncan was in charitable mood after seeing his side steal a dramatic and deserved 120th minute equaliser to set up a replay at Hillsborough in Sheffield on April 22.

"I'm just glad to have another chance, I'm just so proud of the players and the club. When all's said and done it's a marvellous result for us and, not only that, I thought we played good football too.
"(The disputed goal) is all about ifs and buts. To be fair it made no difference to me or anyone else at that point.

"At 2-0 up I never thought anything about victory. Although we were playing well we were never really coping with the talent they had. A 2-0 lead in a normal match isn't enough and it certainly isn't against Juninho and (Fabrizio) Ravanelli."
Robson, clearly despondent after once again witnessing a late Boro capitulation, was in sullen mood.
"I don't think the referee was right to book Kinder and he just couldn't wait to get his red card out of his pocket after the second challenge," he said.
"Chesterfield worked very hard and made it difficult for us but the referee made it more difficult."

The result leaves Boro, assembled at a cost of around 21 million pounds ($34.2 million) in contrast to Chesterfield's 320,000 pounds ($520,000), with a horrendous end-of-season schedule as they fight to win both domestic cups and simultaneously avoid premier division relegation.
It leaves Chesterfield, who have nothing to play for but the F.A. Cup, with their dreams intact.
